title: Airbound: As We May Move
gist: Packy McCormick's deep dive on Airbound (founder Naman Pushp, 21), which bets that carbon-fiber-first, autonomous small eVTOLs built for lowest cost per kg-km can follow a Model T cost curve to displace trucks, vans and cars, scaling across three aircraft (5 kg, 100 kg, 500 kg). The author is an investor and flags major risks: unproven targets, incumbents like Zipline/Uber, and regulation.

themes.theme: Cost per kg-km as sole objective

insights.claim: Airbound optimizes a single loss function, cost per kilogram-kilometer (total cost to build, operate, maintain and refuel an aircraft divided by payload times distance moved over its life), and treats everything else as secondary.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A single metric that arbitrates every engineering trade-off is the tell for a vertically integrated efficiency play; track kg-km cost disclosures as the real KPI.
insights.quote: There is one loss function that we care about: cost per kilogram-kilometer

insights.claim: Naman Pushp argues aerospace and today's drone industry focus on capabilities engineering, while Airbound pursues efficiency engineering: take a well-understood capability set (vertical takeoff, carry a package, deliver) and make it as cheap as possible, reserving novelty for materials and manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If capabilities commoditize, the winner is the lowest-cost operator, which challenges capability-led drone valuations.

insights.claim: Airbound's stated thesis is that if flight can be made cheapest per kg-km, it can dominate 80% of cargo and 90% of human movement; the author explicitly notes success is not guaranteed.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Defines the upside case and the single variable (cost) the whole bet hinges on.
insights.quote: flight can dominate all existing transportation for 80% of all cargo and 90% of all human movement
insights.locator: Airbound: As We May Move (intro to Naman's vision)

insights.claim: Naman believes the eVTOL stack (no runway, autonomy, electric, small) is about 90% of the way to replacing cars, with cost the last 10%; without winning on cost the category is merely 'Aviation++'.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Frames why cost, not capability, decides whether eVTOL becomes mass-market or stays niche.
insights.locator: You Can't Replace a Horse with a Steam Engine

insights.claim: The author argues that when battery replacement cost dominates operating cost at about 100 kg payload, energy becomes the main cost and the only thing left to squeeze is the aircraft itself.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Battery cycle life becomes the key sensitivity; watch cell cost and longevity as the driver of drone logistics unit economics.
insights.quote: we can make it so that energy starts to dominate at 100 kgs

themes.theme: Batching and how transport shaped cities

insights.claim: Historically, cheap transport of bulk inputs set city size: Rome fed a million people via grain shipping (wagon transport about 50x costlier than sea), London grew on coal colliers, New York rose after the Erie Canal cut grain shipping from $100 and three weeks per ton to $10 and six days.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Supports the base-rate argument that step changes in movement cost re-rank geographies and asset values.

insights.claim: Centralizing 'batch machines' (galley, canal boat, railroad, container ship, jet) create hubs because they are only economic when full, while the car, carrying one family point-to-area, spread cities out; the author claims cheap point-to-point flight would expand the map in every direction at once.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A reusable model for second-order effects: batch vehicles agglomerate, individual vehicles disperse; point-to-point flight implies real-estate repricing far from hubs.

insights.claim: Marchetti's Constant (people commute about 30 minutes each way) explains why urban radius grew from about 2.5km in 1800 to about 20km by 1960 but has stalled since; container ships now move slower than under Nixon and planes fly at similar speeds.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Transport speed has stagnated for 60 years, which is the gap Airbound targets and why any real speed gain would be a discontinuity.

insights.claim: Logistics is organized around batching because every mode sits on a cost-speed-versatility frontier; batching forces waiting and pre-positioned capex-heavy locations (warehouses, DCs, depots) whose rent, inventory and labor are amortized into item prices.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If unbatched cheap movement works, the fixed-asset footprint of last-mile logistics (urban DCs) is what gets stranded.

insights.claim: Amazon went from eight warehouses to 54 and cut the average package trip from 450 to 141 miles, showing how much capital is spent pre-positioning inventory to buy speed.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Shows the scale of capex substituted for cheap fast movement; a cheap flying alternative would attack that spend.

themes.theme: Model T analogy: steam carriage to eVTOL

insights.claim: Early steam carriages were effectively buses because their staffing and capex economics required batches of passengers; the Benz (1885) made individual ownership possible but only for the rich, and Ford's Model T won by cost, not performance.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The analogy is the core lens: individual vehicles need a cost-first design lineage, not just a technology unlock.
insights.locator: You Can't Replace a Horse with a Steam Engine

insights.claim: Ford's Model T fell from about 1.5 years of average pay ($850 vs $550) in 1908 to about a fifth of a year's pay ($260 vs $1,350) by 1925 with essentially unchanged engine performance; Ford deliberately traded performance for cost.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Provides the cost-curve template (roughly 8x affordability gain) against which eVTOL price requirements are compared.
insights.quote: any color the customer wants, as long as it’s black
insights.locator: You Can't Replace a Horse with a Steam Engine

insights.claim: Naman views a conventional plane as the 'steam carriage of the sky' and today's eVTOLs as early automobiles; current human-grade eVTOLs cost about $4-5 million to buy and over $1 million to produce.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Anchors the price gap (about 100x to reach car parity) that incumbents like Joby and Archer must close.
insights.locator: You Can't Replace a Horse with a Steam Engine

insights.claim: The author computes that taking a $4-5M passenger eVTOL to car pricing needs about 100x cost reduction, or roughly twenty doublings at Wright's Law 20% per doubling, which is unlikely at $4M demand; this is why Joby and Archer operate flying taxis instead of selling to consumers.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Explains why pushing a cheap small aircraft up the size curve is a structurally different path than pushing an expensive one down the cost curve.

insights.claim: Airbound's bet is to push a sub-$5,000 vehicle up the size curve rather than push a $5M vehicle down the cost curve, funding volume via burritos and blood deliveries before people.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Sequencing (cheap cargo first, humans later) is the strategic distinction to underwrite.

insights.claim: Wright's Law originated in a 1936 study of airplane cost (about 20% labor decline per doubling of cumulative output), yet aviation stayed low-volume with fewer than 10,000 aircraft a year versus about 90 million vehicles in autos.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Aviation has not ridden the learning curve that made solar, batteries and chips cheap; the volume gap is the opportunity and the risk.
insights.quote: The entire aviation industry globally makes less than 10,000 aircraft a year

insights.claim: Naman contends carbon fiber is the third materials paradigm (after natural and semi-natural materials), the first designable from the molecule up, and that industry wrongly treats it as a drop-in metal replacement instead of redesigning aircraft around it.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Core technical differentiation claim; validate via manufacturing cost, yield and weight data as they emerge.

insights.claim: Lighter airframes trigger 'mass decompounding' (smaller battery, fewer or lighter motors, less structure), the reverse of the vicious add-weight loop, and Airbound designs the whole aircraft carbon-fiber-first with design coupled to manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Weight compounding means small structural savings amplify into battery and motor cost savings, driving kg-km cost.

insights.claim: Airbound claims to have pioneered manufacturing an entire aircraft, including internal supports, as a single carbon fiber piece (V2), which removes joins that add weight and labor and enables high-aspect-ratio long wings.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: One-piece composite manufacturing is the potential process moat; the claim is unproven at volume.
insights.quote: What we have pioneered is the ability to make an entire aircraft in one piece

insights.claim: Airbound's in-house composites specialist made the TRT surface from a single layer of roughly 40 gsm carbon cloth, and outside vendors could not work with such light materials, forcing Airbound to build capabilities in-house.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Evidence that the tight design-manufacturing loop creates know-how suppliers lack, supporting vertical integration.

insights.claim: Airbound's V2 uses tilt rotors with wingtip propellers that counter wingtip vortices, acting like a longer wing without the structural cost, and turned out easier to stabilize than the earlier tailsitter TRT.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Shows willingness to add mechanisms when system-level cost per kg-km improves.

insights.claim: The author claims a V2 is more than 60% payload at takeoff versus Naman's rule of thumb of 30% structure, 30% fuel and 30% payload for conventional aircraft, with structure targeted at 4-5% of total weight.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Payload fraction is the efficiency proof point relative to peers.

themes.theme: Airbound vs competitors on specs and cost

insights.claim: Payload-to-empty-weight ratios differ sharply: Amazon Prime Air's drone about 0.06x, Zipline P2 about 0.15x, Airbound TRT 0.67x, and Airbound V2 1.67x (5 kg payload).
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Quantifies Airbound's claimed structural efficiency lead over the incumbents in drone delivery.

insights.claim: V2 costs under $5,000 to make in India and about $1,000-2,000 more with US labor, versus Naman's estimate of about $100k for competitors' drones at Airbound's scale, now mid-to-high tens of thousands.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Unit cost gap is the central claim and rests on Naman's own estimates of competitors, so treat as unverified.

insights.claim: Airbound has completed more than 13,000 autonomous flights across Bengaluru and Guntur and recently flew two V2s and twenty-six TRTs simultaneously, with one operator supervising about five aircraft.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Flight-hour accumulation is the evidence base for both learning curve and regulatory case.

insights.claim: Uber invested in Zipline and signed a deal absorbing all of Zipline's planned production, aiming for a million drone deliveries a day by 2029, while DoorDash (an Airbound investor) builds its own drones.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Incumbent platforms are locking up supply via partnerships, the main competitive risk to a cost-led entrant.

insights.claim: The Medium (100 kg) targets 4-6 cents per tonne-km, below a fully loaded semi at about 7 cents (ATRI $2.34 per mile over 20 tonnes), and about half a cent per km for a full 100 kg; Naman says the payload-cost curve flattens after about 20 tons, so Airbound aims to flatten it at 100 kg.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If 100 kg unbatched flight matches truck economics, trucking's $4-6T market becomes contestable; these are targets, not achieved costs.

insights.claim: Naman expects Medium launch cost of about $20,000 to manufacture and $35-40,000 to buy, and targets under 2 cents per mile for one person and about 3 cents per mile for a family Large, versus AAA's 86 cents per mile for car ownership (29 cents for fuel, maintenance, repairs and tires).
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Targets that exist only in spreadsheets; the gap versus car cost is the size of the claimed opportunity.

themes.theme: Market sizing and Movement Monopoly moats

insights.claim: Trucking is about half of the $8-12 trillion global logistics market, and last-mile delivery was sized at about $167 billion in 2025; the human-movement pool is mostly the car itself ($2.5-3T new sales plus about $2T used) versus about $3T for ride-hailing, public transport and airlines combined.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Shows the TAM logic: to address people-movement you must compete with car ownership cost, not with airlines.

insights.claim: Naman plans to start pitching in 2027 'Replace all of your trucks with my drones. Not some of them, all of them.'
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A dated commercial milestone to monitor for pilots or customer announcements.
insights.quote: Replace all of your trucks with my drones. Not some of them, all of them,

insights.claim: The author argues Airbound could combine Scale Economies, Network Effects (local availability flywheel, owners leasing aircraft like robotaxis) and Process Power, with Naman targeting 'a Boeing moat multiplied by a TSMC moat' plus Uber and DoorDash distribution.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Defensibility depends on reaching scale before incumbents; the network moat is hypothetical until fleet density exists.
insights.quote: a Boeing moat multiplied by a TSMC moat

insights.claim: Illustrative math: a billion movements a day at $1 each is $365B revenue, about $36.5B earnings at 10%, roughly $1.1T at 30x, and would need about 27x Uber's 2025 daily trips; Naman claims a $10 trillion potential, which the author calls insane and not a forecast.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Sets the far-tail valuation frame; the ambition claim mostly matters as signal of founder intent.

insights.claim: Uber handled 13.6 billion rides and deliveries in 2025 (about 37 million a day) with $193B gross bookings and $52B revenue, and Americans made about 232 billion driving trips in 2024.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Base rates for how much movement demand a network business can capture.

insights.claim: Naman argues avionics that should cost tens of dollars sell for tens of thousands only because aviation volumes are tiny, and at automotive scale aviation-grade hardware might cost about 20% more than automotive; he wants suppliers to become Foxconn-like, not Boeing-like.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Volume-driven component deflation is a key lever, and aerospace supplier margins are exposed if a high-volume entrant emerges.
insights.locator: S, M, L Aircraft, XXL Business

insights.claim: Airbound intends to become the largest carbon fiber fabric buyer to induce supplier investment, aims to bring carbon fiber to steel-like cost, and Naman predicted it could become the largest lithium-ion buyer, potentially buying twice as many cells as everyone else combined.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Bravado, but signals demand-pull thesis on materials and cell suppliers if the vision materialized.
insights.locator: S, M, L Aircraft, XXL Business

insights.claim: Airbound cost is very sensitive to battery replacement cost; solid-state batteries (projected 10-100x life of lithium-ion) and structural batteries are research bets that may take a decade, with cracking, loss of contact and dendrites as commercialization hurdles.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Battery longevity is the biggest external lever on drone delivery unit costs; watch solid-state progress.
insights.locator: S, M, L Aircraft, XXL Business

insights.claim: Naman deliberately postpones commercial traction, handoff design and regulation, arguing the bottleneck is getting the tech and economics right first and that cheap demand-rich logistics generates the safety data regulators need; he wants 10 million flight hours of data before flying a human.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A focused but risky sequencing choice: revenue traction is intentionally deprioritized, so commercial milestones lag.
insights.quote: it feels like a waste of time to get commercial traction for the sake of getting commercial traction
insights.locator: Trade-Offs, or Choosing What Not to Do (Yet)

insights.claim: The author and a founder friend raise credible counters: high switching costs and partnerships (Zipline with Uber and Walmart) may matter more than cost, and the market may be a land grab where capability to fly is scarce; Naman replies delivery fees are a huge concern and Uber's strategy is low-cost land grab.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Key bear case: cost may not be the deciding variable if platforms lock in supply and customers.

insights.claim: The author notes a plausible outcome where Zipline, Joby and Archer win in America while Airbound wins in India and similar value-conscious markets, and that it is hard to imagine most movement on one company's platform.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A regional-split outcome is the realistic base case to weigh against the winner-take-most pitch.

insights.claim: Naman argues India's value-conscious culture and demanding delivery expectations (Meesho, Zepto, Blinkit, 45-minute food) make it the ideal place to build cheap ubiquitous flying machines, a 'Made in India, Made for the World' strategy versus Silicon Valley's capability focus.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Explains the geographic edge in cost discipline, though the author admits Indian consumers resist paying for software.
insights.quote: building for value is something that does not exist in Silicon Valley culture but exists in Indian culture
insights.locator: Made in India, Made for the World

insights.claim: Naman says he half-jokingly suggested that if you believe in Airbound you should short Tesla because there is little point to a self-driving car when you can have a self-flying car.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Flagged as half-joking; treat as sentiment, not a tradeable thesis.
insights.quote: If you believe in Airbound, you should short Tesla.
insights.locator: S, M, L Aircraft, XXL Business

insights.claim: Naman says the aircraft can only be designed by one person, and the author cites Fred Brooks on conceptual integrity, arguing a founder-architect who holds the whole system in mind is critical when weight compounds every local decision; this is key-person risk as well as an advantage.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Concentrated design authority speeds coherence but creates single-point-of-failure risk in a 21-year-old founder.
insights.quote: This is the kind of aircraft that can only be designed by one person

insights.claim: Airbound is backed by a $37M Greenoaks-led Series A with Lightspeed and Lachy Groom; the author invested and discloses his own bias, and the founder is 21 with no college degree, who started from a $500 hackathon prize.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Disclosure: the author is an investor, so the piece is advocacy; discount enthusiasm accordingly.
insights.locator: Naman's Vision / Naman Learns to Make Drones
